title: Wisdom to give
tomorrow: Baba hands Simran something wrapped in cloth. what is it?

lines: TELL US WHERE YOU COME FROM.
IS OLD THE SAME AS WISE?
cards: The college essay prompt says: tell us about where you come from. Simran has three versions, and all of them sound like a brochure. Maya says ask your dad.

Harjit says ask Baba. So after dinner she sits on the rug by Baba Kartar's chair with her laptop, and before she can open her mouth Bebe calls from the kitchen: don't ask him, he'll tell you about the first truck again.
He laughs. Her group chat is split the same way. One friend: old people know things you can't search for.
Another: being old doesn't make anyone right.

teach.h: A BOY CALLED THE OLD ONE.
teach.b: Sikhs have a story that sits right on that split. Tradition says a village boy once came to Guru Nanak with questions about death, questions far too big for his age, and the Guru called him Budha: the old one.
He grew up to be Baba Budha, and tradition says he lived to serve the Gurus who came after Nanak, an elder the whole community turned to.

Here's one view, and it's strong. Ask the elders. Sikh memory has long traveled as sakhis, stories told aloud at kitchen tables and in the gurdwara, and an elder is a library you can only borrow from while they're here.
Baba Budha himself became the one people asked. Now the other view, just as strong.
Age isn't the same as wisdom. The boy got the name old one for his understanding, not his years.

And for Sikhs, every piece of advice has a test above any person: Guru Ram Das writes, in paraphrase, the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word. Ang 982. So an elder's counsel is weighed, not just obeyed.
Both views are in one life. Baba Budha was the boy who saw early and the old man people came to.
Simran shuts the laptop. She doesn't ask Baba what to write. She asks what he remembers.
He starts with the first truck.

how: Sikh families pass on sakhis, stories of the Gurus and the community, by telling them aloud; elders are honored and consulted, and Sikhs test any counsel against Gurbani.

o: advice you must follow because it comes from age
a book of rules handed down in the family
what elders carry for the next ones to ask for

games.q: two views, one life — tap the pairs.
p: the old one, a name for a wise boy
stories told aloud and passed down

s: Baba Budha got his name because he was very old
tradition says Guru Nanak called the boy old for his understanding, not his years.
for Sikhs, the Guru's word is the test for anyone's advice
Ang 982: the Word is the Guru, the Guru is the Word.
honoring elders and weighing their advice can't go together
Baba Budha's own story holds both views in one life.

games.q: your uncle insists you take the job he picked for you. your gut says no. both of today's views are at the table. what honors both?
o: do what he says; elders know best, full stop.
ignore him; being older doesn't make him right.
ask what his own choices taught him, then weigh it against what you hold true.
games.why: ask the elders, and weigh what they say. Baba Budha was both the boy who saw early and the elder people came to.

practice: Think of one elder you could ask: a grandparent, a neighbor, an old teacher, a coworker near retirement. Take a pen and write by hand one question for them, not about what you should do, but about their own life.
Fold the paper and keep it somewhere you'll see it.

wordCard.voice: Wisdom to give. Elders carry stories and counsel; Sikhs ask for both, and weigh them against the Guru's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: budha, old one; tradition says Guru Nanak gave the name to a wise boy.

carryVoice: Keep this one: ask the elders what they remember, then weigh it against the Word. That's today.

sources.ref: Baba Budha and Guru Nanak (janamsakhi tradition), retold
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 982 (Raag Nat, Guru Ram Das: 'bani guru guru hai bani'), paraphrased
